question: What does 'raised' convey here?

positions.position: It is a metaphor for causing noble fame and praise.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur says God created the means of Muhammad's reputation; height evokes dignity beyond ordinary reach, grounded in rare virtues and his title al-Amīn.

positions.position: It evokes the Prophet's once weak call becoming powerful and widespread.
positions.reasons: Islahi compares the call with a reverberating roar.

turns_on: The image can describe honorable reputation or the strength of the public call.

question: What does 'for you' add to the wording?

positions.position: Its fronting emphasizes personal benefit, exclusive address and prompt reassurance.
positions.reasons: Bint al-Shati calls this ordinary, purposeful Arabic and quotes Abduh on hastening the good news. Elmalılı contrasts beneficial renown with harmful fame; Islahi hears God's support for him alone. Ibn Ashur says the parallel لك of 94:1 and عنك convey care.

positions.position: It delays specification of the object, producing ambiguity then clarification.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi compare صدرَك, ذكرك and وزرك; Ibn Ashur acknowledges this effect. Bint al-Shati objects that readers join لك to its object and صدرَك already identifies it.

positions.position: It is an insertion that might mark specification, exclusivity or emphasis.
positions.reasons: Bint al-Shati reports these alternatives from al-Nishaburi and rejects the idea that the pronouns are redundant.

positions.position: Its place after removal of the burden continues the verse's rhetorical sequence.
positions.reasons: Al-Alusi cites the conjunction and fronted لك after 94:3; Tabataba'i notes the poetic lift after the burden.

turns_on: The dispute concerns delayed clarification versus ordinary emphatic address and benefit.

question: What does 'remembrance' mean?

positions.position: It means praised reputation, dignity and honorable mention.
positions.reasons: Asad gives primary remembrance and a figurative sense of eminence; Elmalılı calls it honor. Ibn Ashur connects praise with the title al-Amīn. Bint al-Shati cites al-Raghib: remembering may be inward or spoken, recalling the forgotten or retaining it; dhikr often accompanies God's name.

positions.position: It also evokes revelation, the Qur'an and thought.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı cites 21:10. Bint al-Shati contrasts dhikr attached to God's name with al-dhikr for revelation, citing 18:10, 20:14, 20:42, 20:124, 23:11, 38:8, 15:6, 15:9, 54:25, 41:41, 16:44, 25:18 and 36:11.

turns_on: Whether the word here denotes praised renown alone or also hints at scripture.

question: How is the rāʾ in 'your remembrance' pronounced?

positions.position: It is emphatic to match the verse endings.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazari attributes this to Makkī and others for both ذكرك and وزرك; works permitting both say emphasis is more common, and al-Dānī learned it from Abū al-Fatḥ.

positions.position: It is light according to the regular rule.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazari reports this from other authorities; al-Dānī chose it despite learning the emphatic form.

turns_on: Rhyme matching versus the regular pronunciation rule.

question: How was the Prophet's remembrance raised?

positions.position: God joined Muhammad's name with His own in testimony and public worship.
positions.reasons: Mujahid, Hasan, Qatada and the Gabriel report say the two names are joined; Qatada extends this to both worlds. Sources name testimony, adhan, iqama, tashahhud, sermons, festivals, pilgrimage, marriage, letters, public spaces and coins. Hassan's five daily muezzin verses and al-Sarsari's lines illustrate it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and others add Quranic pairings, titles, earlier books and covenants; 9:62, 4:13, 5:92, 4:59, 4:80, 47:33 and 64:12 are cited. Al-Alusi calls pairing the greatest instance.

positions.position: God honored him through prophethood, messengership and rank.
positions.reasons: Yahya ibn Sallam, al-Qushayri and Bursevi stress prophethood. Al-Biqai adds his preprophetic virtues, migration and successive honors. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi include divine titles, equivalent obedience and blessings. Al-Razi adds final prophethood and his name on the Throne.

positions.position: God spread his admirable name and call widely through successive generations.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya says he was already renowned in Mecca. Al-Razi cites followers, reciters, exegetes, preachers, rulers, Sunnah preservation and 19:96; Ibn Ashur cites al-Amin; Qutb describes millions' love; Islahi names pilgrims and Ansar. Abduh says Muhammad rescued nations from superstition and corrupt ideas and restored sound nature. Kur'an Yolu cites 21:107 and worldwide spread.

positions.position: His remembrance was raised among angels and in the Hereafter as well as on earth.
positions.reasons: Mawardi gives an afterlife parallel; Thalabi locates mention among angels; Abu Ali and Qurtubi add angels and believers, the Praiseworthy Station and noble ranks; Qatada speaks of both worlds; Razi includes the Throne and enduring honor.

positions.position: He was announced in earlier books, and earlier prophets were bound to recognize him.
positions.reasons: Thalabi, Baghawi and Ibn Kathir cite the covenant to believe in him and teach their peoples; Qurtubi says his religion will prevail over all. Zamakhshari, Razi and Alusi count earlier books among several means.

positions.position: Blessings upon him and enduring love elevate his mention.
positions.reasons: Razi invokes 19:96; Baydawi, Biqai, Alusi and Elmalılı cite God's and angels' blessings and the duty of believers in 33:56. Study Quran calls blessing the strongest sign; Qutb stresses later generations' love.

positions.position: His standing makes him creation's refuge for intercession on Judgment Day.
positions.reasons: Dhu al-Nun describes Muhammad's aspiration beyond the Throne while other prophets' circle it; creatures seek his intercession. Razi mentions visitors to his resting place and their hope for it.

positions.position: The once weak prophetic call became an unstoppable public voice.
positions.reasons: Islahi says pilgrims at hajj, especially the Ansar, carried the call beyond Arabia.

positions.position: The exact form of elevation is left open.
positions.reasons: Bint al-Shati declines to limit it: the choice of a poor orphan as messenger exceeds worldly ambition. Corpus Coranicum leaves worldly standing versus standing before God unresolved.

turns_on: Sources specify different, sometimes overlapping ways of elevation; Alusi emphasizes the greatest instance and Bint al-Shati declines exact limitation.

question: What follows from joining the Prophet's mention to God's?

positions.position: Faith and worship require acknowledgment of Muhammad as God's messenger.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ata and Tustari say faith is completed by naming him; Ibn Ata says Messenger implies Lord. Ibn Abbas says worship without the testimony brings no benefit and is unbelief. Dahhak says prayer and sermons lack validity; al-Sarsari says this of adhan. Qashani joins both declarations with Islam's completion.

positions.position: Obedience and allegiance to him count as obedience and allegiance to God.
positions.reasons: Razi cites 4:80 and 48:10; Nasafi adds 47:33, 64:12, 4:13 and 9:62. Baydawi, Biqai, Alusi and Elmalılı list the same honor.

positions.position: His community shares in honor through reverent remembrance.
positions.reasons: Razi describes Sunna preservation, greetings and hope for intercession. Biqai cites Razi that the community receives a full share, and reports God's friends are those whose mention or sight recalls God, whose speech adds knowledge and whose conduct prompts detachment.

positions.position: Public renown benefits leaders, while obscurity may benefit private worshippers.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya says God apportions each according to need. A report about an obscure servant is unverified in one version; another says God raised a servant's name.

turns_on: The notes draw different consequences for testimony, obedience, communal honor and the benefit of fame.

question: What did reports say God told the Prophet about his raised mention?

positions.position: Gabriel relayed that whenever God is mentioned, Muhammad is mentioned with Him.
positions.reasons: The Abu Said report is widespread. Ibn al-Jazari names Ibn Jarir, Ibn Hibban and Abu Ya'la; Ibn Ashur says al-Suyuti graded the Ibn Hibban and Abu Ya'la chain hasan while Qadi Iyad cites it without a chain. Mawardi and Alusi state no grading. Some wording reverses the order, saying God's name comes when Muhammad is named. Gabriel asks how the raising occurred; Muhammad answers that God knows best.

positions.position: After comparison with earlier prophets' gifts, God recalled shelter, guidance, enrichment, an opened breast, removed burden and raised mention.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Kathir transmit versions; one adds God took Muhammad as friend. The Anas account adds scripture carried in his community's hearts and the Throne's treasure la hawla wa-la quwwata illa bi-llah. Ibn al-Jazari prefers Anas as explaining his unique distinction.

positions.position: The Prophet directed people to say 'servant' before 'messenger'.
positions.reasons: Abd al-Razzaq and Tabari transmit this order; Ma'mar explains it. The Prophet also forbade excessive praise like Christian praise of Jesus.

positions.position: A tangential report defines backbiting as true disliked speech and slander as false disliked speech.
positions.reasons: Al-Itqan cites Abu Hurayra; the note gives no connection to this verse.

turns_on: The reports differ in setting, wording and added gifts to the Prophet or his community.

question: When and where was the raised remembrance evident?

positions.position: It was already spread in Mecca.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya says his name had become known through the earth then; Ibn Ashur and Biqai trace its causes to childhood virtues and al-Amin.

positions.position: The adhan is a future fulfillment relative to Meccan revelation.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya notes that the adhan began in Medina, so the verse anticipates this instance.

positions.position: The verse reflects the public spread of Islam through Arabia and beyond.
positions.reasons: Islahi names hajj pilgrims and the Ansar; Kur'an Yolu also allows an early promise of later worldwide reach.

positions.position: Its scope includes this world, heaven and the Hereafter.
positions.reasons: Qatada says both worlds. Qurtubi names angels, believers, the Praiseworthy Station and noble ranks; Razi says the honor continues until Resurrection.

turns_on: The timing of the Medinan adhan relative to Meccan revelation and the verse's reach beyond earthly life.

question: How does this blessing connect with the surrounding verses and sūrahs?

positions.position: The sequence of gifts consoles the Prophet and promises support.
positions.reasons: A divine reminder lists shelter, guidance and enrichment with expansion, burden removal and raised mention. Ibn Atiyya says this consoles him against Quraysh and implies victory; Abu Hayyan similarly sees victory and later ease against mockery. Ibn Ashur reads relief for distress: Hira, revelation, Abu Talib's protection, conversions and promises, citing 26:3, 2:272 and 93:5. Biqai places inward completion before public honor.

positions.position: Sūra 94 completes Sūra 93, with subsequent blessings after earlier favors.
positions.reasons: Asad dates it almost immediately after al-Duha. Islahi distinguishes pre-Islamic and early prophetic favors from later success and materialized predictions. Study Quran contrasts Sūra 93's external needs with Sūra 94's spiritual relief and closing commands.

positions.position: Some reciters treated the two sūrahs as one unit.
positions.reasons: Asad reports Tawus and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz reciting without a second basmala, citing Razi; Study Quran reports a similar Companion practice.

positions.position: The verse's position after the burden's removal heightens its effect.
positions.reasons: Al-Alusi cites the conjunction and لك after 94:3; Tabataba'i hears a poetic lift. Ibn Ashur says رفعنا and وضعنا coordinate with نشرح, which lam has shifted to the past.

positions.position: Raised remembrance is a special distinction of the sūra.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazari suggests this and prefers the Anas report, which adds the Quran-bearing community and the Throne's treasure.

positions.position: The address extends through the Prophet to every true follower.
positions.reasons: Asad gives the broader address; Islahi traces inner expansion, relief from hardship, mission completion and disciplined success.

turns_on: Sources relate the verse to prior favors, later ease, the preceding sūra or a unique distinction.

question: Where was this sūra revealed?

positions.position: Most say Mecca, shortly after Sūra 93.
positions.reasons: Study Quran reports the majority; Asad says it came almost immediately after Sūra 93.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas says Medina.
positions.reasons: Study Quran attributes this view to him.

positions.position: Some assign only verses 5–6 to Medina.
positions.reasons: Study Quran reports this narrower assignment.

turns_on: Whether all, none, or only verses 5–6 are Medinan.

question: What grammatical observations accompany the cited discussion?

positions.position: An accusative verbal noun can stand for an omitted action verb.
positions.reasons: Sibawayh analyzes ما أنت إلا سيرا this way in statements and questions. Interrogative أقياما and أطرَبا describe a present state; أغدة وموتا and Jarir's question imply verbs; أعبدا may instead be vocative. شرب الإبل is not a transitive act upon camels for this nunation.

positions.position: A nominative verbal noun can serve directly as predicate.
positions.reasons: Sibawayh contrasts إنما أنت سير without a verb, citing al-Khansa's إقبال وإدبار and نهارك صائم وليلك قائم; accusative with an omitted verb remains possible.

turns_on: Implied verb with accusative versus direct nominal predication.

question: What outside texts are compared with this verse?

positions.position: Psalm 145:14 describes the Lord supporting the fallen and raising the bowed down.
positions.reasons: Neuwirth proposes the comparison without asserting dependence.

positions.position: Some read al-Takwir 81:19–21 as describing Muhammad, a noble and trusted messenger.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur reports the possibility alongside the Prophet's honorable mention.

turns_on: The notes offer distinct comparisons without deciding their relationship to this verse.
